newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto party may boycott after electoral rout.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto party may boycott after electoral rout.

text.p: Pakistan's ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto, routed at the polls by her main rival Nawaz Sharif, may reject the results and boycott national and provincial assemblies, party sources said on Tuesday.

The sources, speaking at her home in the village of Naudero in the southern province of Sindh, said Bhutto would hold a meeting of leaders of her Pakistan People's Party (PPP) in Islamabad on Wednesday to decide the party's strategy.
With 85 results declared for the 217-seat National Assembly (lower house), the PPP had won only three seats, against 62 for the Pakistan Muslim League (PML) led by Sharif.

Cricketer-turned-politician Imran Khan's Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement) had won no seats. A breakaway PPP faction led by Ghinwa Bhutto, Lebanese-born widow of Bhutto's slain brother Murtaza, had also failed to gain a seat.
The Karachi-based ethnic Mohajir National Movement (MQM) had won six seats and the Awami National Party, based in North West Frontier Province and allied to the PML, had gained eight.
Most of the seats declared were from populous Punjab, where the PML was also sure to dominate the provincial assembly.
Turnout was low at Monday's elections at the end of a lacklustre campaign during the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan.
The PPP sources, who asked not to be named, said the party felt there had been widespread rigging and irregularities, and might decide to boycott the national and provincial assemblies.
"The pressure on Benazir is that her defeated candidates cannot believe the results, so the party will probably stay away from the assemblies in protest at the rigging," one said.

An air of gloom settled over Bhutto's farmhouse at Naudero as results broadcast on state television showed the extent of the electoral disaster for the PPP. "It's unbelievable, just unbelievable," muttered one depressed party official.

President Farooq Leghari called the elections after sacking Bhutto's government on November 5, citing corruption, nepotism and other abuses. Bhutto, who was due to leave Naudero for Islamabad later on Tuesday, denies the charges.
The MQM also complained of election irregularities and intimidation by the breakaway MQM-Haqiqi faction.
But the head of a Commonwealth team of observers said the voting had been free and mainly peaceful.
"We are satisfied that all those who wished to vote were able to do so and express their own wishes at the ballot box," former Australian prime minister Sir Malcolm Fraser said.
Nevertheless, 10 people were killed in election day violence around the country, officials said.
PML officials in Sharif's home city and provincial capital Lahore said that, based on their projections, the party could get up to 130 seats, which would be a huge defeat for Bhutto.
"We are winning from all over the country," Sharif told cheering crowds outside his home on Monday evening.
Qazi Hussain Ahmad, leader of the religious Jamaat-i-Islami, which boycotted the polls, said voter apathy had vindicated his party's rejection of the "corrupt electoral process".
